w:r.w:t: GAT-MADRL: Topology-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Congestion Control in SDN
Aditya Kumar Maurya, Vimal Kumar, Sanjay Kumar
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Madan Mohan Malaviya University of Technology, Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh 273010, India

Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the control plane from the data plane and gives the controller a network-wide view, which makes global congestion control possible for the first time. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches to SDN congestion control mostly waste that view. They flatten the network state into a vector of link statistics, discard the topology, and assume a single agent, so they neither generalize to unseen topologies nor represent how congestion spreads from one link to the next. This paper proposes GAT-MADRL, which addresses all three limitations. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) encoder with edge features and a temporal LSTM embeds switches and links directly from the SDN topology graph. A cooperative actor–critic architecture assigns one agent per controller; agents choose flow paths and queue weights from local observations, while a centralized critic with a counterfactual baseline trains them under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). A congestion-propagation attention module represents queue build-up spreading across path-coupled links, which is what makes the controller anticipatory rather than reactive. The prototype runs on Mininet, Ryu, PyTorch and PyTorch Geometric over a REST/WebSocket interface. Across fat-tree, Abilene-like wide-area and multi-domain edge topologies, GAT-MADRL cuts 99th-percentile flow completion time by 15–25% and packet loss by 31–45% against the strongest baseline, holds packet delivery ratio above 99%, keeps control-loop latency at 7–9 ms within a 50 ms epoch, and limits cross-topology degradation to 18–24% where flat-state baselines degrade by 88–115%.
Software-defined networking; Congestion control; Deep reinforcement learning; Graph attention networks; Multi-agent reinforcement learning; Traffic engineering; Quality of service; OpenFlow

Networks that once linked a handful of machines now carry cloud services, video, gaming, real-time trading and machine-to-machine traffic at volumes that have grown by orders of magnitude in two decades. The mix has also changed: short, bursty, latency-sensitive mice flows share links with long-lived elephant transfers. Congestion control has been studied for more than thirty years, from Jacobson's TCP congestion avoidance [8] through CUBIC [9], BBR [10] and DCTCP [11]. Every one of these algorithms runs at the endpoints and infers the state of the network indirectly, from loss, ECN marks [15] or round-trip-time samples. None of them can see the network. Each sender optimizes for itself on partial information.

SDN [1, 3] removes that constraint. Separating the control plane from the data plane and centralizing it in a controller with a network-wide view together with OpenFlow [1, 2] and mature controllers such as Ryu [5], ONOS [6] and OpenDaylight [7] makes fine-grained traffic engineering and real-time policy configuration practical. What it costs is a much larger design space. Paths, load balancing, queueing discipline and per-flow rate limits all have to be chosen continuously, and hand-written
heuristics for that space are brittle: they work in the setting they were tuned for and degrade elsewhere.

The architecture has three planes. Switches in the data plane match packets against flow-table entries and consult the controller on a miss; the control plane installs and maintains those entries; the application plane hosts routing, security and traffic-engineering services above the controller's northbound API. For congestion control this gives the controller four levers that end-to-end schemes lack: reroute individual flows around a

hot link, spread load over non-shortest paths, retune per-port queueing parameters, and read utilization, queue-occupancy and per-flow counters from every switch at fine granularity. Active queue management sees only one queue; telemetry-driven schemes such as HPCC [16] need data-plane modifications.

Casting the controller as a deep reinforcement learning agent [22, 23] is therefore a natural move, and there is encouraging work in that direction. Three problems persist. First, the state is almost always a flat vector of link utilizations and queue occupancies, which throws away every relation between links and switches; the resulting policy does not transfer to a new topology and cannot reason about how a hot link affects its neighbours. Second, nearly all prior work is single-agent, whereas production deployments run several controllers arranged hierarchically or geographically [57, 58], and per-flow control at scale carries well-known flow-management overheads [61]. Third, most methods are reactive they respond once queues have already built up.

Applying DRL here is also awkward for reasons specific to the domain. Exploration has to be cautious, because a bad action drops customer traffic. Reward design is delicate, since a careless objective produces pathological policies. Traffic is non-stationary on long time scales, so policies drift. Real network data is expensive to collect, which pushes training into emulation. And the whole control loop must fit inside tens of milliseconds per decision epoch while respecting the stability and fairness properties the networking community has spent decades establishing.

The research problem is therefore: given an SDN operated by one or more logically linked controllers, with flows arriving at varying rates, sizes and latency targets, design a congestion-control framework that
monitors global network state continuously and at high granularity;
encodes that state so the relational structure of the topology is preserved, letting the learner reason about the spread of congestion;
chooses paths and per-link queue configurations that minimize packet loss and tail flow-completion time;
executes in a decentralized manner consistent with multi-controller deployments while exploiting centralized information during training;
runs within the tens-to-hundreds-of-milliseconds time constants of traffic control.

Three developments make this tractable now. Graph Attention Networks [40, 41] consume graphs directly and produce structure-aware outputs. Multi-agent reinforcement learning under CTDE [53, 56] has become stable enough for cooperative training. And SDN controllers together with the Mininet emulator [4] are mature enough to build realistic experiments against conventional baselines.

Topology-aware MARL formulation. Congestion control in SDN is modelled as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP) [52] over a graph-structured state space, with full definitions of states, observations, actions, rewards and transitions.

GAT-MADRL framework. A cooperative actor–critic combining a shared GAT encoder (edge features plus a temporal LSTM), per-agent actors over local subgraphs, and a centralized critic with a counterfactual baseline, trained with multi-agent PPO [56].
Congestion-propagation attention. An attention mechanism over path-coupled links that supplies an inductive bias for proactive control and yields readable attention maps.
End-to-end prototype. A modular implementation bridging Mininet [4], Ryu [5], PyTorch [66] and PyTorch Geometric [67] through a documented REST/WebSocket interface, packaged for reproducibility.
Evaluation. Three topologies, six baselines and six metrics, with paired significance testing over five seeded runs [78, 79, 80].

Organization of the paper. Section II reviews related work and states the research gap, Section III develops the formulation and the framework, Section IV covers the prototype, the experimental design and the results, and Section V concludes.

Prior work on network congestion spans four decades and several research communities. It is reviewed below in six parts: classical congestion control and queue management, learning-based congestion control, graph neural networks in networking, multi-agent reinforcement learning, the systems and measurement context, and a comparative analysis that states the research gap.
A. Classical congestion control and queue management

Jacobson [8] introduced slow start and congestion avoidance and set the loss-based end-to-end paradigm. CUBIC [9] grows the window along a cubic curve and was the Linux default for over a decade. BBR [10] estimates bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation time rather than reacting to loss, and DCTCP [11] uses ECN marks [15] to keep data-centre queues short. On the queue side, RED [12] drops probabilistically to smooth bursts, CoDel [13] attacks buffer bloat by marking on packet sojourn time rather than queue length, and PIE [14] is a lightweight proportional-integral controller of queueing delay. HPCC [16] and PowerTCP [17] push per-flow rate control to nanosecond granularity using in-band telemetry from P4 switches [59].

All of these act on local, indirect signals. An SDN controller can retune RED thresholds network-wide, but standard AQM still works one port at a time and cannot exploit knowledge of alternate routes or cross-link coupling. The data-plane precision of HPCC and PowerTCP is complementary to the global routing intelligence developed here, and combining the two is left for future work.

Nguyen and Armitage [18] surveyed early ML for traffic classification and Wang et al. [19] the broader ML-for-networking workflow. Mao et al. applied DRL to resource management [20] and then to adaptive video streaming with Pensieve [21]. On congestion control specifically, Remy [35] generated algorithms automatically, Aurora [34] trained a PPO agent to update the congestion window from throughput, latency and loss, PCC Vivace [37] took an online-learning route, and Pantheon [36] provided a common training ground. Within SDN, Deep-RMSA [38] handled routing and spectrum assignment in optical networks, CFR-RL [39] posed traffic engineering as RL, AuTO [70] scaled DRL to data-centre traffic optimization, and Xu et al. [71] proposed experience-driven networking. The underlying algorithms are the standard DRL toolkit: DQN [23, 24] with double Q-learning [25], dueling networks [26] and prioritized replay [27], plus policy-gradient
methods A3C [28], PPO [29] with GAE [30], DDPG [31], TD3 [32] and SAC [33]. What almost all of these share is a flat state vector and a single agent.
C. Graph neural networks in networking

Kipf and Welling [40] popularized graph convolutional networks, GraphSAGE [43] generalized them to inductive settings, and Gilmer et al. [44] unified the field under message passing. GATs [41] learn per-edge attention coefficients; GATv2 [42] improved their expressiveness. In networking, RouteNet [45, 46] showed that GNNs predict per-path delay and jitter and transfer to unseen topologies, and RouteNet-Erlang and RouteNet-Fermi extended it [47, 48]. Almasan et al. [49] paired DRL with a GNN encoder for routing optimization and demonstrated the generalization benefit of topology-aware state. These remain single-agent, and none of them models congestion propagation between links explicitly.

Tan [50] contrasted independent and cooperative learners and Busoniu et al. [51] surveyed the field; Oliehoek and Amato [52] formalized the Dec-POMDP used here. MADDPG [53] introduced the CTDE paradigm, COMA [54] proposed counterfactual multi-agent policy gradients, QMIX [55] handled value factorization, and MAPPO [56] showed that PPO works surprisingly well in cooperative settings. MAPPO is the training backbone of this work. MARL has seen limited application to networking, and to the authors' knowledge no prior work combines it with GNN-based topology encoding and congestion-propagation attention for SDN congestion control.

Several systems have instrumented SDN for fine-grained measurement: SIMON [72] for sensing and inference in data centres, the survey of Yassine et al. [73] on measurement challenges, and software-defined latency monitoring [74]. DevoFlow [61] identified the scalability limits of fine-grained flow management, which is precisely the argument for a multi-agent design in which each controller handles only its own subgraph. Onix [57] and Kandoo [58] describe distributed control platforms in production, underlining why a congestion-control framework must scale as controllers are added.
F. Comparative analysis and research gap
Table 1 compares the main families against the proposed framework on state representation, agent count, attention, topology generalization and emulation realism.
Comparison of the primary techniques against the proposed framework.

Four gaps follow. Most DRL congestion-control algorithms lack topology awareness, which costs them generalization and sample efficiency. Multi-agent formulations are missing even though real SDN networks run multiple distributed controllers [57, 58]. Congestion propagates along the topology, yet no reviewed study models that effect explicitly. And packet-level emulators such as Mininet [4] and Ryu [5] are poorly integrated and documented in existing work, which limits reproducibility.

This section defines the system model, represents the network as a graph, states the traffic model and congestion measures, formulates the control problem as a Dec-POMDP, and then develops the GAT-MADRL framework that solves it.

The data plane is a set of OpenFlow switches connected by point-to-point links. The control plane holds one or more controllers running, for example, Ryu. Each switch reports to exactly one master controller; standby controllers exist for fault tolerance. Controllers communicate over a control-plane network assumed reliable and much faster than the congestion-control loop.

Hosts attach at edge switches, and traffic moves as end-to-end flows described by source and destination host, ports, protocol, arrival time, byte count and a QoS class expressing latency and throughput requirements. F(t) is the set of flows in the network at time t. Routing and rate decisions are made in control epochs of duration Δt, in the range 10–100 ms. At the start of each epoch every controller polls its switches for OpenFlow statistics, exchanges summaries with peers as needed, and installs the chosen actions before the next epoch begins. The epoch is the unit of time for the reinforcement learning problem.
Switches are OpenFlow 1.3 compliant and expose per-port and per-flow statistics pollable at intervals no longer than Δt.
The control plane is reliable: controller–switch messages arrive in order with bounded delay below Δt.
Topology is known through LLDP or configuration and changes on time scales much slower than the control epoch.
The number of learning agents equals the number of controllers; with one controller the framework reduces to the single-agent case.
Flow arrivals are stochastic and may be non-stationary, but the generation rate changes slowly relative to the epoch.
The algorithm operates at layer 4 and above and does not modify endpoint transport parameters. It influences flow performance indirectly, through routes and per-link queue configuration.
The system model, illustrating the assumptions listed above.
B. The network as a graph

The topology is a directed graph G = (V, E) with N = |V| switches and M = |E| directed links. Each edge (u, v) carries a capacity c_uv, a buffer b_uv and a propagation delay d_uv. Virtual edge switches represent host attachment points.

Each link has a state vector h_uv(t) holding utilization ρ_uv(t), queue occupancy q_uv(t), loss rate ℓ_uv(t) over the last epoch and aggregated per-flow statistics; H(t) stacks these and is the primary input to the agents. Each node v carries x_v(t) with switch-level metrics: flow-table capacity and fullness, CPU utilization where available, and ingress and egress rates. Together they form the network state at time t.

G supplies the connectivity consumed by the GAT encoder. For node v, the neighbourhood N(v) is every u with an edge in either direction. Both directions matter: forward propagation spreads overload from a hot path onto alternates, and backward propagation carries back-pressure toward the source.

Flows arrive as a non-homogeneous Poisson process with time-varying rate λ(t); each arrival carries a descriptor (src, dst, size, class). Size is drawn per class. Mice flows have long-tailed distributions largely confined to hundreds of kilobits; elephants are heavier-tailed and reach hundreds of megabytes. The QoS class fixes the flow's tolerance for latency and loss: latency-sensitive classes pay a large penalty for queueing delay and a small one for reduced throughput, and throughput-sensitive classes the reverse. These weights enter the reward directly.

An admitted flow follows the route the algorithm selects. Without intervention, flows take the Dijkstra shortest path, the default OpenFlow behaviour. The system can override this by installing flow-table rules for a different route. Mid-flow rerouting is permitted but penalized, since constant path changes hurt TCP.
D. Congestion measures and the cost function

Congestion is measured at three levels. At link level, utilization ρ_uv(t) is traffic carried in epoch t over capacity c_uv; a link is congested when ρ_uv exceeds a threshold (default 0.8) or when q_uv(t) > 0.6 b_uv, and ℓ_uv(t) is the fraction of packets dropped on the link during the epoch. At flow level, congestion appears as queueing plus propagation delay, packet loss, reduced throughput and a long flow completion time (FCT); the 99th-percentile FCT of mice flows is the standard tail-latency indicator in data centres. At network level it is summarized by delivered throughput, global loss ratio, maximum link utilization, the fraction of links above the utilization threshold, and the variance of utilization across links.
These combine into one scalar per epoch. With non-negative weights α₁…α₅ summing to one:
C(t) = α₁·MaxLinkUtil(t) + α₂·Loss(t) + α₃·MeanFCT(t) + α₄·P99FCT(t) + α₅·Churn(t)

Churn(t) is the fraction of active flows that changed path during the epoch. The reward r(t) is the negative of this cost. The α weights encode operator priorities; the default configuration weights tail latency and loss most heavily (Table 3).
E. Problem formulation as a Dec-POMDP

Congestion control is formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process, the standard model for cooperative multi-agent problems under partial observability [52]. The tuple is ⟨I, S, {A_i}, P, R, {O_i}, Z, γ⟩, where I is the set of agents (one per controller), S the state space, A_i the action set of agent i, P(s′|s, a) the transition kernel under joint action a, R(s, a) the shared reward, O_i the observation space of agent i, Z the observation model and γ the discount factor.

State. The state s_t comprises the topology G, all link vectors h_uv(t), all node vectors x_v(t), the active flow set F(t) with parameters and progress, and switch queueing state that is not directly observable. This space is very large; compressing it is the job of the GAT embedding.

Actions. Agent i controls routing and queue management on its own switches. When a new flow arrives at one of them, the agent picks a path from K_max candidates enumerated offline with a k-shortest-paths algorithm, so every candidate is loop-free and K_max stays small (4–8 in practice). It also picks per-port queue weights from W discrete configurations. The action of agent i is thus (path_assignments_i, queue_weights_i), and the joint action is their concatenation. The joint action space is the product of the individual spaces and grows fast, which is why policy-gradient methods are used rather than value-based ones.

Observations. Agent i sees its own switches and links, traffic on them, and summary statistics from adjacent controllers; it has no direct visibility into distant controllers. Its observation at time t is o_i,t, and the learned policy π_i must depend only on that. Under CTDE the critic may still consume the full state s_t during training.

Transitions. P(s_{t+1}|s_t, a_t) is determined by the joint routing action, new flow arrivals, the progress of existing flows, queueing dynamics at every link, and disturbances such as link failures. It is stochastic and non-stationary over long horizons, though approximately stationary within a training episode, and it has no closed form: transitions are sampled from the emulator, as is standard for model-free RL.

Reward. r(t) = −C(t) + β·ShapingTerm(t), where the shaping term penalizes states known to be dangerous, such as queue occupancy above 90% of buffer size, before they cause loss. β is set conservatively so shaping does not bias the policy.

Objective. The joint policy π = (π₁,…,π_n) maximizes the expected discounted return J(π) = E_π[Σ_t γ^t r(t)], subject to each π_i depending only on o_i. Training uses finite episodes of length T and approximates the return by sample averages. Letting the critic see the full state and joint action during training is what makes credit assignment tractable.

GAT-MADRL is a cooperative multi-agent system with one agent per SDN controller, a single network-wide reward, and CTDE training. At run time each agent acts on its own observations; during training a centralized critic sees the topology graph and the joint action and computes the advantage. Four components, shown in Figure 2:
A GAT state encoder, instantiated in both actors and critic with most parameters shared, which turns the topology graph with per-link features into node- and link-level embeddings.
A per-agent actor that takes the embedding of the agent's local subgraph and emits path assignments for new flows and queue-weight settings for its ports.
A centralized critic that takes the whole-graph embedding and the joint action and returns a state-action value for the advantage.
A congestion-propagation attention module over the GAT embeddings, which supplies the inductive bias for anticipating spread.
Training uses a MAPPO variant built on this architecture. Inference uses only the actors; the critic is discarded, as CTDE allows, which is what makes deployment fully distributed.

The GAT-MADRL framework: the shared GAT encoder used by both actors and critic, the per-agent actors, the centralized critic (training only, discarded at inference under CTDE), and the congestion-propagation attention module.
The encoder converts raw SDN telemetry into embeddings that respect the topology.

Per-link features on edge (u, v): utilization ρ_uv ∈ [0, 1]; instantaneous queue length q_uv normalized by buffer capacity b_uv; a smoothed queue length Q_uv,t = (1 − β_q)Q_uv,t−1 + β_q q_uv,t with β_q ≈ 0.1; packet loss rate ℓ_uv ∈ [0, 1]; the number of active flows n_uv normalized by the maximum over edges in the current state; the fraction of flows in each QoS class; and the static properties c_uv and d_uv, each scaled by its network-wide maximum.

Per-node features on switch v: flow-table occupancy, ingress and egress rates, an indicator of which agent manages v, and a one-hot node identifier. The identifier is used during training only and dropped at deployment so the policy does not memorize node identities. All numerical features are standardized using statistics computed over the training episodes, and those statistics are exposed through the inference API so scaling is identical at deployment.
The encoder stacks L GAT layers, L = 3 by default. For node v, the layer-(l+1) embedding aggregates neighbour embeddings under attention:

with W^(l) a linear projection, σ a LeakyReLU of slope 0.2, and the coefficients given by α_vu^(l) = softmax_u( a^(l) · [ W^(l)h_v^(l) ‖ W^(l)h_u^(l) ‖ e_vu ] ), where a^(l) is a learned attention vector and e_vu the edge feature vector. Including e_vu in the attention computation is the departure from standard GAT: attention then depends on link state, not only on topology, so the encoder can distinguish a congested neighbour from an idle one. Each layer uses four attention heads, concatenated at intermediate layers and averaged at the last.
G.3 Edge embeddings and temporal integration

Actions concern links, so link embeddings are needed. A single-hidden-layer MLP with ReLU produces e_uv^(L) = MLP( h_u^(L) ‖ h_v^(L) ‖ e_uv ). Node and edge embeddings share a latent space, or the node embedding is linearly mapped into it.

Temporal context comes from an LSTM placed between the raw features and the GAT. The per-link feature vector at step t is concatenated with those at steps t−1 … t−τ, with τ = 4 by default, and the LSTM emits a fixed-dimensional representation that becomes the GAT input. The agent can then read a rising queue as rising rather than as a single snapshot.

Agent i holds a policy π_i(·, θ_i). Its input is the embedded subgraph of the nodes it controls, their incident edges and one-hop neighbours, with the associated edge embeddings. The network has two heads.

Path-selection head. For each new flow arriving at a controlled switch, candidate paths (enumerated offline) are represented by averaging the edge embeddings along each path. An MLP maps each path representation to a logit and a softmax over the logits gives a categorical distribution.

Queue-weight head. For each controlled port, the head takes the corresponding edge embedding and emits a categorical distribution over W weighted-fair-queueing configurations. The configurations are combinations of per-QoS-class weights, with W = 6 in the reported experiments (Table 3).
The actor samples from each distribution and hands the result to its controller, which encodes it as OpenFlow messages.

Locality. The actor sees only its own nodes and links plus one-hop neighbours. Information from further away arrives through the encoder: after L = 3 layers of attention propagation, each node carries information from up to three hops. This keeps the design compatible with distributed control practice, bounds inter-controller communication, and — for the topologies studied — turns out to be enough, as the ablation on L confirms.

The critic is used only in training and therefore sees the entire state. It runs its own copy of the GAT encoder over the whole graph and also consumes the joint action a, returning V(s, a) for the advantage A_i(s, a).

Architecture. Node and edge embeddings are pooled into a graph-level embedding h_agg = Σ_v β_v h_v + Σ_(u,v) γ_uv e_uv, with β_v and γ_uv learned by the pooling layer using attention weights computed as in the GAT. h_agg is concatenated with one-hot encodings of each agent's chosen path and queue configuration and passed through a three-layer MLP.

Counterfactual baseline. Following COMA [54], credit is assigned by marginalizing over agent i's own action while holding the others fixed: B_i(s, a_i) = Σ_{a′_i} π_i(a′_i | s) · V(s, (a′_i, a_{−i})). The advantage is then A_i(s, a) = V(s, a) − B_i(s, a_i), which isolates agent i's contribution from the joint outcome.

This is the most distinctive part of the design. Congestion rarely stays put: a growing queue on one link lengthens queues upstream through back-pressure and pushes flows onto alternate paths, loading those in turn through ECMP or other load balancing. A useful controller anticipates that spread instead of chasing it.

Formulation. For a link (u, v), the module learns a propagation embedding p_uv = Σ_{(x,y) ∈ PathNeighbours(u,v)} β_(uv,xy) · e_xy, where PathNeighbours((u, v)) is the set of links sharing at least one active flow with (u, v), identified from the OpenFlow statistics cached at each controller, and β_(uv,xy) is a learnable propagation attention coefficient.

Integration. p_uv is concatenated with the GAT edge embedding e_uv before both are passed to the actor and critic. Because propagation adds an embedding rather than changing the interface, the downstream input shape is unchanged and only the encoder module needs modification.

Interpretability. Training produces an attention map over link pairs that operators can inspect to see how congestion tends to travel. In the fat-tree and Abilene-like topologies these maps were readable: attention concentrates on the aggregation-core tier, and jams lower in the hierarchy show upstream coupling. Section IV.C.7 gives the details.

Algorithm. Training uses MAPPO, which is stable in cooperative settings and easier to tune than A3C or SAC. Critics are centralized; each agent learns its own decentralized actor. The actor loss combines the clipped PPO surrogate [29] with an entropy bonus:
L_actor(θ_i) = E_t[ min( r_t(θ_i)·A_i,t , clip(r_t(θ_i), 1−ε, 1+ε)·A_i,t ) ] + β·H(π_i(·|s_t))
Here r_t(θ_i) is the probability ratio between new and old policy for the sampled action, with ε = 0.2 by default. The critic minimizes L_critic(ϕ) = E_t[(V_ϕ(s_t, a_t) − R_t)²].

Experience collection. Parallel workers each run a Mininet instance with a Ryu application. An episode spans T = 256 epochs of length Δt, roughly 12.8 s of emulated time at Δt = 50 ms. Each episode resets Mininet to the target topology and draws a fresh traffic seed. Advantages and returns are computed by generalized advantage estimation [30] with λ_GAE ≈ 0.95. Parameters are then updated by minibatch SGD with K_epochs of 4–10 per buffer, using Adam with warm-up and decay.

Inference. Each controller needs only its actor and the encoder. Per epoch it polls OpenFlow statistics from its switches, exchanges aggregated state with neighbouring controllers over UDP or TCP, builds and normalizes the feature vectors, computes h_v, e_uv and p_uv, runs the actor on its local subgraph, and applies the highest-probability action greedily — flow rules for paths, queue-config messages for weights, with CoDel as the default discipline in the software switch. It then sleeps until the next epoch. On the workstation used here the whole cycle takes under 10 ms per epoch across all controllers, comfortably inside a 10–100 ms budget.

Complexity. Encoder inference costs O(L·(N+M)·d² + L·M·d) per epoch; each agent's actor costs O(K_max·d + |S_i|·W·d), where K_max is the number of candidate paths, d the hidden dimension and |S_i| the number of switches the agent controls. For a fat-tree with 20 switches, 64 links, d = 64, L = 3, 4 heads and 6 ports per switch, this is roughly 10 MFLOP per epoch — tens of milliseconds even on a CPU. The critic's O((N+M)d) applies only during training and does not affect inference.

The prototype has five parts: Mininet topology and traffic-generation scripts, a custom Ryu controller application exposing telemetry and accepting actions, the GAT-MADRL agent in PyTorch and PyTorch Geometric, the REST/WebSocket interface between them, and the training infrastructure that orchestrates parallel emulators and learners.

Everything is Python 3.10, which is the common ground between the SDN ecosystem (Ryu, Mininet) and the deep-learning one (PyTorch). Table 2 lists versions. The repository separates topo/, controller/, agent/, training/, evaluation/, configs/ and notebooks/, with a Makefile providing targets for starting the emulator, the controller and the agent.
A.2 Mininet topologies and traffic generation

Mininet [4] builds hosts as Linux network namespaces joined by veth pairs, with Open vSwitch [69] instances speaking OpenFlow 1.3 to an external controller. Three topologies were implemented: a k = 4 fat-tree with 16 hosts and 20 switches, a 12-node Abilene-like wide-area network, and a multi-domain edge topology of 8 clusters around a small backbone. In the fat-tree, host-to-edge and edge-to-aggregation links run at 100 Mbps, aggregation-to-core links at 1 Gbps, and every link adds 0.1 ms of propagation delay.

Elephant flows are generated with iperf3 and mice with a Python Poisson generator. A YAML file configures per-class arrival rates, size distributions and source–destination patterns (uniform, hot-spot or all-to-all), including configurations derived from published measurements of Google data-centre traffic [62]. A control script starts Mininet, loads the topology, launches Ryu with the custom application, connects the agent over REST/WebSocket and starts the traffic generators; a shutdown script reverses this and cleans up OVS bridges and namespaces.
The application, TopoAwareCongestionApp, subclasses ryu.base.app_manager.RyuApp and does three things.

Topology discovery. It subscribes to EventSwitchEnter, EventSwitchLeave, EventLinkAdd and EventLinkDelete and maintains the topology as a NetworkX [68] graph. Any change triggers a TopologyUpdate over the WebSocket channel so the agent can refresh its own view.
Statistics polling. Every Δt = 50 ms (configurable) it issues OFPPortStatsRequest and OFPFlowStatsRequest to

each managed switch and writes replies into an in-memory table. Per-link utilization is derived from successive port counters divided by capacity and elapsed time. Requests are pipelined over Ryu's asynchronous event model so the controller never blocks on replies, and missing samples from a switch that fails to answer are interpolated rather than treated as errors.

Action execution. Actions arrive from the agent as JSON over the WebSocket. A path assignment becomes a set of OFPFlowMod messages to the switches along the chosen path. A queue-weight action becomes OFPQueueGetConfig plus OF-CONFIG messages, or OFPMeterMod-based rate limiting on switches that cannot reconfigure queues at run time.

The agent is built on PyTorch [66] with PyTorch Geometric [67] for the GAT layers, split into: encoder.py (GATEncoder: stacked GATv2Conv layers, edge embedding, temporal LSTM), propagation.py (CongestionPropagationAttention, multi-head scaled dot-product attention over a sparse path-incidence matrix), actor.py, critic.py, mappo.py (training loop), policies.py (a unified Policy wrapper for inference) and buffer.py. GATv2Conv [42] is used in place of the original GAT formulation because it resolves the per-edge attention ambiguity of the latter. Modules run in eager mode by default; torch.compile gives roughly a 30% inference speed-up in our measurements but is not needed to reproduce the results.

Three message types cross the boundary. Telemetry messages go controller to agent each epoch, carrying the topology graph (only when it changes), per-link and per-node feature vectors and the flows that arrived in the previous epoch; slow-moving features are sent as deltas. Action messages go agent to controller each epoch with path assignments and queue-weight configurations. Control messages, in either direction, cover session setup, configuration changes, agent state queries and shutdown.

Telemetry and actions use the WebSocket to minimize overhead; control messages use REST because human readability matters more there than bytes. JSON was chosen over Protocol Buffers or MessagePack for debuggability, and a production deployment would want the binary format.

Latency budget. On the fat-tree testbed a single epoch breaks down as roughly 8 ms of OpenFlow polling, 1 ms of controller-to-agent serialization and transmission, 4 ms of agent computation on GPU, 1 ms back, and 6 ms to install the resulting OpenFlow actions — about 20 ms in total against a 50 ms budget.

A master process spawns Mininet instances with their controllers and agents. Each instance lives in its own network namespace, and several can share a host as long as the OVS daemon keeps up. Agents accumulate gradients through a lightweight PyTorch DDP parameter server. Hydra [76] manages hyperparameters, with one configuration file per topology and run; each session logs to Weights & Biases [77] and writes local TensorBoard files. Training ran on a workstation with an NVIDIA A100 (40 GB), with emulator and agent on the same machine.

Reproducibility rests on five measures: seeds are fixed and logged in the configuration files; the stack is containerized with separate Docker images for emulator, controller and agent, orchestrated by Docker Compose; the code is released under an MIT-style license with setup instructions; trained checkpoints ship alongside the code so inference-time results can be reproduced without retraining; and the synthetic traces come from public distributions with their generating seeds recorded.

The experiments answer five questions. How does GAT-MADRL compare with conventional baselines (ECMP, SPF, heuristic adaptive routing) across topologies and traffic patterns? How does it compare with AI baselines (DQN, PPO, GNN-DRL single-agent)? How well does it transfer to an unseen topology? Is its inference latency small enough for a real control loop? And what do the attention maps reveal about congestion structure in SDN?
The design crosses three topologies, six traffic patterns, seven algorithms and six metrics. Every combination was run five times with independent seeds, and comparisons use paired t-tests.

Fat-tree. The canonical k = 4 fat-tree [60]: 4 core switches and 4 pods, each pod holding 2 aggregation and 2 edge switches, with each edge switch serving 2 hosts. That gives 20 switches, 16 hosts and 32 bidirectional (64 directed) switch-to-switch links. Host and edge links run at 100 Mbps, aggregation-to-core at 1 Gbps, propagation delay 0.1 ms throughout.

Abilene-like wide area. Modelled on the Abilene research backbone [75]: 12 switches representing major US cities and 30 directed links, with bandwidths from 1 Gbps on regional links to 10 Gbps on intra-coast backbone links and propagation delays from 1 ms within a region to 40 ms coast to coast. The traffic matrix comes from a gravity model calibrated to population and economic activity.

Multi-domain edge. Eight edge clusters around a central backbone. Each cluster has 4 edge switches serving 8 hosts each; the backbone is 4 core switches in full mesh. That is 8×4 + 4 = 36 switches, 256 hosts, 256 host-to-edge links, 12 bidirectional intra-cluster and backbone-facing links and 6 bidirectional backbone links. One agent governs each cluster, giving 8 agents — this is the scalability test for the multi-agent design.

Data-centre mix (fat-tree). Following measurements of production data centres [62, 63], about 80% of flows are mice (≤ 100 KB) carrying 5% of the bytes, while 5% are elephants (≥ 1 MB) carrying 80% of the bytes; medium flows make up the rest. Interarrival times are exponential with λ chosen so that naive shortest-path routing would drive utilization to about 60%. Two source–destination patterns are used: uniform random, and a hot-spot pattern sending 20% of traffic to one popular destination and 20% to a second.

Wide-area gravity model (Abilene-like). Each node pair (i, j) generates flows as a Poisson process with rate λ_ij = K·D_i·D_j / d_ij², where D_i is demand at node i, taken from US city populations, d_ij is the travel time and K is fitted empirically [64, 65]. Flow sizes are log-normal with a mean of 10 MB, giving roughly 45% average utilization under shortest-path routing.

Edge flash crowds. The edge topology runs baseline uniform random traffic plus flash-crowd events: two randomly chosen hosts each begin generating 200 elephant flows of 100 MB. This is the direct test of whether proactive control pays off when demand spikes locally.

A dual-socket AMD EPYC 7543 server, 32 cores and 64 threads, 256 GB DDR4, one NVIDIA A100 40 GB, running Ubuntu 22.04 LTS on kernel 5.15; software versions as in Table 2. Background processes were idled. To reduce variance, cgroups pinned dedicated cores to the emulator, the controller and the agent separately, the GPU was reserved for the agent, and Mininet namespaces were confined to their own bridge so emulated traffic never mixed with host traffic.
ECMP. The default of most forwarding hardware: hash the five-tuple across equal-cost shortest paths. Implemented in Ryu as a simple rule installer.
SPF. All traffic on the hop-count shortest path, with ties broken deterministically by switch ID — approximately what a default OpenFlow network with a learning-switch application does.

Heuristic adaptive routing. Monitors per-link utilization and moves traffic off links above 80% utilization onto the least-utilized second-shortest path. This stands in for competent hand-engineered traffic engineering.

DQN routing. A double DQN with prioritized replay over a flat vector of link utilizations and queue lengths, a 4-layer MLP of width 256, choosing among the K_max candidate paths. Representative of a large share of the DRL SDN routing literature.
PPO routing. The same flat input with an actor and critic of width 256, representing policy-gradient approaches to SDN routing.

GNN-DRL single-agent. The closest existing approach: a GCN encoder with a single-agent PPO actor–critic. It lacks the propagation attention, the multi-agent formulation and the temporal LSTM, which is what makes it the right reference point for isolating those three contributions.

Six metrics are reported. Average end-to-end goodput is delivered bytes over experiment duration, in Gbps, higher being better. P99 FCT is the 99th percentile of flow completion time, the tail-latency indicator that matters most for the mice flows dominating data-centre workloads. Packet loss ratio is dropped over generated packets, taken from OVS port counters. Average queue length is the mean per-link queue over links and epochs, meaningful only at high load. Controller–agent inference latency is the wall-clock interval from telemetry message to action, reported as median and 99th percentile. Cross-topology generalization gap is the relative increase in P99 FCT when an agent trained on topology A runs on topology B, relative to an agent trained on B.

Each configuration of topology, traffic pattern and algorithm was run five times with independent seeds; tables report the mean with standard deviation in parentheses. Comparisons use paired t-tests at α = 0.05 and are called significant only when the test passes and Cohen's d [80] is at least 0.5. For claims of overall superiority across the six baselines, Bonferroni correction sets the per-comparison level to α/6 = 0.0083; reported p-values are uncorrected and the correction is applied at interpretation. Confidence intervals are bootstrap percentile intervals with 10,000 resamples, chosen over parametric intervals because P99 FCT and inference latency have non-Gaussian tails.

Average episode return follows the same three phases on all three topologies: fast improvement over roughly the first 50 iterations, slower gains to about iteration 300, then a plateau. The fat-tree converges fastest, which its regular structure would predict; the multi-domain edge topology takes longest, since eight agents have to coordinate. Wall-clock training time was about 18 hours for the fat-tree, 14 for the Abilene-like network and 28 for the edge topology. Most of that is Mininet emulation rather than gradient computation, so hardware supporting parallel emulation would cut it by roughly a factor of four. Each topology was trained once and the resulting policy reused for all evaluations. The three topologies are analysed in turn below.
Table 4 reports the fat-tree results under the data-centre traffic mix, as mean ± standard deviation over five trials.
Performance on the fat-tree topology (data-centre traffic mix). Bold = best per column.

Three things stand out. GAT-MADRL is best on both P99 FCT and packet loss, roughly 20% and 35% better than GNN-DRL, the strongest baseline. The throughput margin is thin, which fits the topology: a fat-tree has ample bisection bandwidth, so tail latency rather than raw throughput is the binding constraint. And its inference latency of 7.2 ms at P99 is higher than the simpler methods but still well inside the 50 ms epoch.

Paired t-tests put the difference between GAT-MADRL and every AI baseline at significance α = 0.05 for both P99 FCT and loss. Effect sizes against ECMP and SPF are large (d > 1.5); against the other AI methods they range from medium to large (d between 0.6 and 1.2). The ranking survives Bonferroni correction over the six comparisons.

Normalized five-metric performance profile on the fat-tree topology (outer edge = best observed value per metric; from Table 4). GAT-MADRL leads on all quality metrics while paying the highest control overhead.
The wide-area case has a larger diameter, longer and more varied propagation delays, and candidate paths extending to six hops, which changes the problem the agents face.
Performance on the Abilene-like topology (gravity-model traffic). Bold = best per column.

GAT-MADRL again leads on every quality metric. The P99 FCT improvement over the best baseline is 15%, smaller than on the fat-tree, which is what one would expect when there are fewer alternate paths to exploit. The loss reduction holds at 31%. Inference latency rises slightly because each agent covers more nodes and links here.
This is the real test of the multi-agent design: eight agents cooperating, with traffic combining uniform baseline flows and flash-crowd events.
Performance on the multi-domain edge topology (baseline traffic plus flash crowds). Bold = best per column.

The margin is widest here. P99 FCT falls 25% (98 ms against 131 ms for the nearest competitor) and loss falls 45% (0.78% against 1.42%). The edge topology offers the most room for inter-agent coordination and the most benefit from acting before a flash crowd saturates a cluster, so this is where a topology-aware multi-agent controller should win by the largest margin — and does.

Inference latency is also at or slightly below that of the GNN-DRL single agent, because each GAT-MADRL agent processes only 4 switches and their neighbours while the single agent must encode all 36. The parallelism of the multi-agent formulation buys latency as well as quality.

Figure 4 places the three topologies side by side. The ordering of methods is stable across all of them: the two static schemes are worst, the heuristic and the flat-state learners occupy the middle, and GAT-MADRL is lowest everywhere. Absolute values differ by roughly a factor of three between the fat-tree and the Abilene-like backbone, which reflects propagation delay rather than control quality, since the wide-area paths are simply longer. What matters is the relative gap, which widens from 20% on the fat-tree to 25% at the edge as the number of agents and the opportunity for coordination grow. Error bars over five trials do not overlap between GAT-MADRL and any baseline on any topology.
Average end-to-end goodput across topologies, from Tables 4–6.

Figure 5 gives goodput, where the spread is narrower. On a fat-tree with ample bisection bandwidth there is little headroom to recover, and the 0.3 Gbps margin over GNN-DRL is close to the trial-to-trial variation. The gap grows on the Abilene-like and edge topologies, where capacity is genuinely scarce and path choice therefore determines how much of it is usable. Goodput is the metric on which GAT-MADRL wins by the least, which is what the objective predicts: the framework optimizes tail latency and loss, and throughput follows only where those are the binding constraint.
Packet loss ratio across topologies, from Tables 4–6.

Figure 6 shows the same ranking in packet loss, with wider margins. GAT-MADRL keeps loss below 0.8% on all three topologies while the static baselines exceed 2% on two of them, and the reduction against the strongest baseline is 35% on the fat-tree, 31% on the Abilene-like backbone and 45% at the edge. The edge case is the most informative: flash crowds produce exactly the transient build-up the congestion-propagation module is designed to anticipate, and rerouting before buffers saturate converts what would otherwise have been drops into marginally longer paths.

Cross-topology generalization gap in P99 FCT (%).
Cross-topology generalization gap, from Table 7. GAT-MADRL degrades by 18–24% on an unseen topology; the DQN baseline degrades by 88–115%.

This is the clearest single argument for topology-aware state. GAT-MADRL loses about 20% when transferred; the flat-state DQN loses close to 100%, which is to say its policy falls back to something near random because nothing it learned refers to the structure it now faces. A 20% gap is a real cost, not a free transfer, but it is small enough that the transferred policy is a useful initialization for fine-tuning on the destination network.

Routing and control overhead: P99 control-loop latency on the fat-tree topology.
Controller–agent inference latency breakdown, from Table 8. The GAT encoder forward pass dominates at 2.6 ms of the 7.2 ms end-to-end budget.

The encoder is the largest single cost at 37%, consistent with the complexity analysis in Section III.K. OpenFlow polling is second, driven mostly by round-trip time to the switches; everything else is small. Three optimizations are available and untried: caching encoder output while network state is roughly unchanged would save 2–3 ms in steady state, torch.compile cuts the encoder forward pass by about 30%, and batching polls of several switches into one OpenFlow transaction would reduce polling cost. None of these are used in the reported numbers; all are documented in the repository.
Performance against control overhead on the fat-tree topology, combining P99 FCT (Table 4) with inference latency (Table 8).

Because both the encoder and the propagation module are attention-based, the learned weights can be read off the topology. On the fat-tree the map shifts with load: at low utilization attention is close to uniform across edges; as utilization rises it concentrates on links into the aggregation switches; under a synthetic burst it narrows further onto a handful of aggregation-core links. That matches the standard analysis of fat-tree bottlenecks, so the model recovers known structure without being told it. On the Abilene-like topology the propagation maps show East Coast links coupled to one another through westbound traffic, and regional links coupled to their local neighbours. For an operator, this interpretability is worth as much as the latency numbers: it turns the controller into something whose decisions can be inspected.
Five variants of GAT-MADRL, each removing one component, were run for a fixed 6 hours on the fat-tree under moderate traffic with the pattern of Section IV.B.2, all for equal training time.
Ablation study on the fat-tree topology, P99 FCT (ms).
Ablation study on the fat-tree topology, from Table 9. Removing propagation attention costs +13.7% P99 FCT; replacing GAT with GCN costs +17.0%.

Every component earns its place. The multi-agent formulation matters most: collapsing it to a single agent costs 24.7% and reduces the system to the GNN-DRL baseline used in the comparison above. Choosing GAT over GCN is worth 17.0%, since selective attention over neighbours is the right inductive bias for learning which links interact. Propagation attention accounts for 13.7%, the temporal LSTM for 10.5%, and the counterfactual baseline for 7.3%. The individual degradations sum to about 73%, far more than any combined effect could plausibly be, so the components overlap in what they contribute rather than adding independently — several of them are partly compensating for the same missing information.

RQ1, classical baselines. GAT-MADRL leads on every quality metric on all three topologies. P99 FCT improvements range from 28% (against the heuristic on Abilene) to 54% (against SPF at the edge), and packet loss falls 61–74% against ECMP. The advantage is largest on the edge topology, which has the most devices and therefore the most room for the multi-agent design and for acting early.

RQ2, AI baselines. GAT-MADRL beats DQN, PPO and GNN-DRL on all quality metrics. Against the flat-state agents the gain is 15–35% in P99 FCT and 30–45% in loss. Against GNN-DRL — which already has a graph encoder — the remaining 15–25% gap in P99 FCT is attributable to the multi-agent formulation, the propagation attention and the temporal LSTM, in that order of magnitude according to the ablation.

Tail-latency reduction achieved by GAT-MADRL relative to each baseline on every topology, computed from Tables 4–6.

RQ3, generalization. This is where the difference is starkest. DQN degrades by about 100% when moved to an unseen topology; GAT-MADRL degrades by about 20%, which indicates a representation that refers to structure rather than to particular nodes.

RQ4, latency. P99 inference latency was 7–9 ms on every topology, comfortably inside a 50 ms budget, with room left over. If more headroom were needed, the optimizations of Section IV.C.6 — cached attention, JIT compilation, parallel polling — are the obvious next steps.

RQ5, attention. The maps recover the topology's real bottleneck structure and vary with traffic conditions: near-uniform at low load, concentrated on the links most likely to congest at high load and during bursts. This gives operators a diagnostic view of what the controller is reacting to, which is a practical benefit independent of the performance numbers.
Below about 20% load, GAT-MADRL is no better than the simple baselines, which achieve similar latency at a fraction of the complexity. The framework earns its cost on busy networks.

GAT is expensive relative to the problem on small networks. On topologies below roughly 8 switches, simple baselines matched it on FCT while running far faster. The target is networks of tens to hundreds of nodes.

Training is hardware-hungry: about 18 hours per topology on a single-A100 workstation. In production this implies either continual learning or scheduled retraining windows, and possibly dedicated hardware at each aggregation point so some agents can keep learning while others are updated.

The results assume a reliable control plane. That assumption fails under a deliberate attack on the control channel or a control-software fault, and a compromised or slow control link could lead the framework to install wrong configurations. A safety-constrained variant that falls back to a fixed hand-engineered policy when the control plane degrades is an important next step.

All results come from Mininet. It reproduces packet-level behaviour well, but hardware deployments add vendor-specific controller interfaces, hardware queue constraints and control-channel overheads such as TLS handshakes.

GAT-MADRL couples a shared GAT encoder carrying edge features and a temporal LSTM with per-agent actors, a centralized critic using a counterfactual baseline, and a congestion-propagation attention module, trained with multi-agent PPO under CTDE. A complete Mininet–Ryu–PyTorch prototype was evaluated on fat-tree, Abilene-like and multi-domain edge topologies against six baselines. It held packet delivery ratio above 99% everywhere, cut 99th-percentile flow completion time by 15–25% relative to the strongest baseline, delivered the highest goodput, kept control overhead within 7–9 ms of a 50 ms epoch, and reduced the cross-topology generalization gap from roughly 100% to about 20%.

Five directions follow. Federated and multi-domain training would let domain agents exchange model parameters instead of raw traffic histories, sharing what is learned without exposing sensitive data. Integration with P4-programmable hardware [59] would supply fine-grained in-band telemetry and move state collection into the data plane, cutting polling overhead. Safety-constrained learning through constrained MDPs or shielded RL would bound the damage a policy can do during training and under distribution shift — a prerequisite for production use. Online and continual adaptation, using non-stationary replay buffers and change-point detection, would let agents track traffic drift without full retraining. Finally, deployment on commercial switch hardware such as Tofino-based systems would require accounting for device-specific behaviour, hardware queue constraints and OAM rules, and would naturally extend to encrypted QUIC traffic and 5G/6G slicing.
